results.why: Deck B packs much denser, higher-quality interaction: 4 No More Lies, Three Steps Ahead, 3 Get Lost, 4 Lightning Helix, Day of Judgment and Inevitable Defeat. Resonating Lute gives it a strong ramp-and-refuel engine, and Traumatic Critique and Jeskai Revelation give it flexible finishers. Deck A spends slots on weaker cards like Flashback, Firebending Lesson and a lone North Wind Avatar, and with only 2 No More Lies it has thinner protection against threats.

Deck A's suite is tighter and more powerful. Resonating Lute pairs with Jeskai Revelation and the card-draw package, Get Lost is premium flexible removal, and six counters plus Traumatic Critique give it real answers to everything. Deck B's mana and black sources are a bit better, but singleton North Wind Avatar, Flashback, Tablet of Discovery and a thinner counter suite are clearly weaker choices, while A's mana is still functional.

Deck B is a coherent mana-creature ramp shell. Elves, Pollinator, Spider Manifestation and Bloom Tender power out Ouroboroid, Balloon Man copies and Craterhoof, Nature's Rhythm and Formidable Speaker find the payoffs, and the manabase supports its colors. Deck A mashes together an underpowered Stormchaser's Talent/Boomerang package and a ramp core with few payoffs, plus a lone Jolly Balloon Man with almost no red sources, so its plan doesn't hang together.

Deck A is a coherent green ramp list. It has 30 creatures, plenty of mana dorks and Nature's Rhythm, and closes games with real payoffs in Craterhoof, Ouroboroid and Balloon Man copying Gearhulk. Deck B is 61 cards and splashes a single Balloon Man with almost no red sources, so its pile of bounce and blink value has no clear way to win.

Deck B pairs the Dwarf-and-Equipment engine (Kíli, Dáin's Company, Giott, Mauler) with seven cheap burn spells, so it can actually interact and clear blockers. Its equipment is efficient: Jitte double strike, Mattock's free attach, Dáin Ironfoot's Axe token. Deck A runs dead weight like Doc Ock's Tentacles with no creatures of mana value 5 or more, has zero interaction, and leans on a clunky 4-drop plan.

Deck A plays two Sundown Pass, a Crimson Vow land that rotated out of Standard in 2024, so it isn't legal as listed. Deck B is a legal and coherent Dwarf equipment shell. It has cheap, impactful equipment (Lavaspur Boots, Dragonfire Blade, Leyline Axe), Thorin, Mountain-king as a payoff, and a sound 23-land manabase with Cavern and Lonely Mountain support.

Deck A is a proven Golgari-style sacrifice shell. Cheap fodder (Freebooter, Inspector, Pollinator, Clues) fuels Rottenmouth Viper, Sackville-Bagginses and Obsessive Pursuit, and Lively Dirge adds recursion on top. The red splash for Biotech Specialist is a bit greedy but supported by Starting Town, shocks and Pollinator. Deck B is a coherent mono-black aristocrats deck, but its threats are low-impact and it lacks a finisher on the level of Viper.

Deck B is the stronger, more proven shell. Cheap artifact and creature fodder (Gene Pollinator, Callous Inspector, Freebooter, Clues, Landers) feeds Rottenmouth Viper, Obsessive Pursuit and Sackville, Lively Dirge adds recursion, and the dual lands plus Starting Town make the splash workable. Deck A's mono-black mana is clean, but it relies on low-impact 1/1s and drain triggers with no real finisher, and some of its inclusions (like Bloodghast) look questionable for Standard legality.

Deck B is a coherent Boros superfriends shell. It pairs cheap interaction (Burst Lightning, Get Lost, Helix, Sear, 4 Solitary Cell) with a planeswalker curve and Voice of Victory to protect the walkers, and its two-color mana is clean. Deck A is a pile of half-plans: Caretaker's Talent and Way of the Pyromancer alongside Day of Judgment, which wipes its own tokens, plus a 1-of Chandra and The Mind Stone, a top-heavy curve, and colorless or tapped utility lands that strain the mana.

Deck B is a cohesive superfriends control shell. Day of Judgment sweeps while the walkers stay safe, and Caretaker's Talent turns Elspeth, Ajani and Fountainport tokens into card draw. Way of the Pyromancer and Gideon's Memorial ramp toward the top end. Deck A splits between Voice of Victory aggro and a pile of walkers topped by three 6-drops, so its plan holds together less well, though B's colorless lands do strain its mana somewhat.

Deck A is a focused mono-green Nykthos ramp deck: four Nykthos, Badgermole Cub doubling dork mana, Spider Manifestation, and Ba Sing Se feed X-tutors like Nature's Rhythm and Invasion of Ikoria. Those tutors find a strong toolbox of top-end threats, including Bahamut, Emrakul, Craterhoof and Titan. Deck B halves its Nykthos count and spreads into midrange value pieces (Kiora, Trailblazer, Life's Legacy), giving it a weaker mana engine and a less explosive payoff.

Deck B is the tighter mono-green Nykthos ramp shell. It runs four Nykthos, Spider Manifestation (which untaps when you cast four-drops and up), and Ba Sing Se to fuel enormous mana. Nature's Rhythm and Invasion of Ikoria tutor into a real toolbox of finishers: Craterhoof, Emrakul, Bahamut and Titan. Deck A splits its slots across Ouroboroid, Trailblazer, Kiora and only two Nykthos, so it has less explosive mana and fewer game-ending payoffs for its Fight Rigging and tutors.

Deck A is essentially the established Boros Heroic shell. It pairs Illuminator Virtuoso and Favored Hoplite with efficient red pump spells like Monstrous Rage and Ancestral Anger, which hand double strikers trample and give much more explosive kill turns. Its 20-land Boros manabase is aggressive but functional. Deck B is a coherent mono-white heroic list with clean mana, but its lower damage output and lack of trample make it the weaker tournament choice.

Deck A is a cohesive mono-white heroic list with 18 creatures and a healthy protection suite (Gods Willing, Feat of Resistance, Sejiri Shelter) to blank removal. Its 19 lands include 2 MDFCs, and the mana is clean. Deck B has the stronger individual cards in Monstrous Rage and Swiftspear, but it runs only 14 creatures and 20 lands plus Spikefield, has almost no way to protect its targets, and pays a lot of life to its mana base.

Deck B is the more complete control shell. No More Lies, Sear, Get Lost, Supreme Verdict and The Wandering Emperor give it answers to both threats and spells, while Deck A has no counterspells and leans on Fiery Impulse, Erode and clunky sweepers. B's mana is also better built for black: six real black sources from triomes and shocks support Inevitable Defeat, whereas A's black depends on the conditional Gloomlake Verge and Shattered Sanctum.

Deck B is essentially the established Jeskai Revelation shell: cheap Fiery Impulse and Erode to survive the early turns, Farewell and Together as One as late-game catch-alls, and a 27-land base built around Great Hall and fast lands that rarely enters tapped. Deck A's No More Lies and Verdict package is playable but leaves it thinner on one-mana interaction. Its mana is also clunkier, with five tapped triomes and off-color shocks like Watery Grave and Blood Crypt used only to splash black for Inevitable Defeat.

Deck A is a coherent, proven Simic Spells shell. Up the Beanstalk rewards discounted Crabs and Terrors, while Boomerang Basics and This Town Ain't Big Enough rebuy Beanstalk and Talent, and its 18 lands cast everything cleanly in two colors. Deck B adds a three-color manabase only to run Bushwhack, with just 8 green sources and only 3 basics to fetch, so it gets slightly better removal at the cost of shaky mana and a weaker card-advantage engine.

Deck A is a tight Izzet delve-threat tempo shell with a light green splash. It runs efficient cantrips to fuel Terror and Crab, plenty of cheap removal (Fiery Impulse, Burst Lightning, Axe, Critique), and some countermagic, on a solid 19-land, three-color manabase. Deck B has a cute Beanstalk/bounce engine with five- and seven-drops, but it offers almost no real interaction beyond tempo bounce and Bushwhack fights, so it is far easier to punish in a real field.

Deck B runs four Faithless Looting, which is banned in Modern, so it isn't tournament-legal as written. Deck A is a coherent mono-black Archon reanimator. It has redundant enablers in Stitcher's Supplier, Overlord, Street Wraith and Troll, plus Persist and Emperor of Bones to bring Archons back, and Phyrexian Tower and Crypt of Agadeem as backup ways to hardcast them. Its mana is clean and its disruption package is sensible.

Deck A runs four Faithless Looting, which is banned in Modern, so it isn't tournament-legal, and its loot engine collapses without it. Deck B is a legal, coherent mono-black Archon reanimator list. Overlord, Supplier, Street Wraith and Troll fill the yard, Persist and Emperor of Bones bring Archon back, Phyrexian Tower and Crypt of Agadeem provide fast mana, and the mana base is clean.

Deck A is the tuned Eldrazi ramp shell. Green Sun's Zenith, Fanatic of Rhonas and Dryad Arbor give consistent turn-two acceleration, and Fanatic's ferocious mana pairs with Trudge and Mycospawn. Ugin, Eye of the Storms and Ulamog are a stronger top end, with MDFC lands and Disciple adding card flow, while Deck B relies on weaker ramp like Talisman of Impulse and Sire of Seven Deaths.

Deck B is the tuned Trudge/Eldrazi ramp shell. Fanatic of Rhonas and Green Sun's Zenith give consistent fast mana and access to Trudge and Dryad Arbor, and Ugin plus Ulamog are much stronger payoffs than Sire and a lone Devourer. Deck A leans on Utopia Sprawl with only nine Forests, plus clunky Talismans and Turntimber, so its ramp is less consistent and its top end is weaker.

Deck A is a coherent Riddlesmith/Daredevil artifact-storm list. Does Machines and Artist's Talent loot Echo of Eons into the graveyard and rebuy Baubles. Ancient Tomb and Urza's Saga give it fast mana, Defense Grid protects the combo turn, and Gamble finds the win. Deck B half-borrows that engine but cuts the looting and recursion enablers, which leaves 3 Daredevils and 3 Echoes as clunky cards next to a generic Dark Ritual/Infernal Tutor shell that lacks Ad Nauseam-style payoffs.

Deck B is the established Legacy artifact-storm shell. It uses Urza's Saga and Ancient Tomb for fast mana, Does Machines and Artist's Talent to loot and rebuy artifacts with Echo of Eons, and Gamble into a cheap red Grapeshot finisher, with Defense Grid and Squelcher as protection. Deck A splices a Dark Ritual/Tendrils storm package onto the Riddlesmith/Daredevil engine with too few artifacts to support Mox Opal, so its plan is less coherent and its kill is clunkier.

Deck B has eight ways to bin Phoenixes (Buried Alive plus Faithless Looting), so its core plan shows up far more often. It also packs plenty of free or one-mana spells (Mutagenic Growth, Gut Shot, Lava Dart with flashback, Bolt) to hit three instants and sorceries in a turn. Deck A leans on only four Buried Alive and dilutes the plan with a clunky 3-mana Fantasticar package, so it is less consistent at actually returning Phoenixes.

Deck A is a focused Legacy Phoenix list. Buried Alive and Faithless Looting bin the Phoenixes, and the free spells (Mutagenic Growth, Gut Shot, Lava Dart) plus cantrips make three instants/sorceries in one turn easy to hit. It also has burn for reach and Force for protection. Deck B splits between a 3-mana Fantasticar plan and a Phoenix plan with fewer cheap enablers and no discard outlet beyond Buried Alive, so its combo turns are less consistent.

Deck A is a focused, synergistic mono-white go-wide list. Free 0-drops, Springleaf Drum and cheap Inspectors power out Leonardo, Spider-Man, Search Party Captain and Salt Road Packbeast for card advantage and big swings, Ramosian Rally provides free reach, and 14 lands of perfect mana suit its low curve. Deck B has premium burn but plays like a payoff-light Boros artifact pile with 18 lands, no Kuldotha Rebirth or similar engine, and scattered one-ofs and two-ofs, so it floods more and pressures less.

Deck A is a coherent Boros Kitty shell: Glint Hawk and Kor Skyfisher bounce artifacts for value, Ardent Recruit and Galvanic Blast reach metalcraft off the artifact lands, and Bolt, Blast and Journey give it real interaction. Deck B is a mono-white go-wide pile with no removal. It runs filler like Phyrexian Walker and has no way to answer opposing threats, so a strong player would much rather register A.

Deck A is a coherent Boros Snacker-style shell. Sneaky Snacker is never cast; it is discarded to Thrilling Discovery, Pursue the Past and Faithless Looting, then returned by drawing three cards. Spirit Mascot and the Eidolons feed on that loop, and Tireless Tribe with Inside Out plus Escape Tunnel or Fling gives a real combo kill. Deck B is an unfocused Boros aggro pile that plays clunky 4-mana Eidolons and card-filtering spells with little payoff for its discards.

Deck A is a coherent Boros aggro deck with a solid curve, real removal (Bolt, Journey, Lava Dart) and a clean 18-land Boros manabase. Deck B splices a Tireless Tribe/Inside Out combo onto Eidolon and Sneaky Snacker value. It runs only one Fling, plays Snacker off reanimation alone with no blue or black mana, and spends slots on looting rather than a focused kill. That makes it far less consistent.

Deck B is a coherent Survival/Rector engine. Survival, Karmic Guide, Deranged Hermit, Symbiotic Wurm, Squee and Goblin Bombardment give it real recursion, sacrifice value and a way to win, with Birds and fetchlands smoothing a five-color base. Deck A is a pile of Rector targets and card draw with almost no win condition beyond three Krosan Tuskers. Its Explorer-plus-Decree plan is slow and clunky, so B is far more tournament-worthy.

Deck A is a coherent Survival of the Fittest toolbox. Rector, Pattern and Karmic Guide recur value creatures, and Goblin Bombardment both sacrifices them and closes the game. Its sac outlets, card advantage and mana fixing (Birds, fetches, City) all line up with the plan. Deck B is a muddled Rector/Decree control shell with almost no win condition beyond hardcasting Krosan Tusker, and filler like Gaea's Blessing and Innocent Blood leaves it far weaker overall.

Deck A is a coherent Survival/Sneak Attack build. Survival finds Nicol Bolas, Dragon Tyrant or Colossus, and Sneak Attack slams them with haste, so their upkeep costs never matter. It is backed by discard and a deep green-red-black mana base with 8 dorks. Deck B's reanimation package is fast but its target suite is weak: Bloodfire Colossus costs 8 life off Reanimate and its sacrifice also hits you for 6, and Survival is awkward with few green sources.

Deck A is a focused reanimator list. Dark Ritual, Buried Alive, Survival and Putrid Imp fill the graveyard, and twelve reanimation spells can put a 13/13 Bloodfire Colossus into play on turn 1–2, backed by Cabal Therapy. Deck B's Sneak Attack/Survival toolbox is slower, relying on a 4-mana enchantment, and its three-to-four-color mana with only a few red sources is stretched. Off-color pieces like Phantom Nishoba and Nicol Bolas make it clunky.
